segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Now about the collection for the holy ones: you too should do as I directed the assemblies of Galatia.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: On the first day of every week, each of you should put something aside at home and save it up, in proportion to how you have prospered, so that no collections have to be made when I come.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: And when I arrive, I will send whomever you approve, with letters, to carry your gift to Jerusalem.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: If it seems worthwhile for me to go as well, they will travel with me.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: I will come to you after I pass through Macedonia—for I am passing through Macedonia—

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: and perhaps I will stay with you for a while, or even spend the winter, so that you can send me on my way wherever I go next.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: For I do not want to see you now only in passing; I hope to stay with you for some time, if the Lord permits.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: But I will stay on in Ephesus until Pentecost,

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: for a great door for effective work has opened to me, and the opponents are many.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: If Timothy comes, see that he has nothing to fear while he is with you, for he is doing the Lord’s work just as I am.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: So let no one look down on him. Send him on his way in peace, so that he may come to me, for I am expecting him with the brothers.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Now about our brother Apollos: I strongly urged him to come to you with the brothers, but he was not at all willing to come now. He will come when he has the opportunity.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Stay alert, stand firm in the faith, be courageous, be strong.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Let everything you do be done in love.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: I urge you, brothers and sisters—you know the household of Stephanas, that they are the firstfruits of Achaia and have placed themselves at the service of the holy ones—

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: to place yourselves in turn under people like these, and under everyone who shares in the work and labors at it.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: I rejoice at the arrival of Stephanas, Fortunatus and Achaicus, because they have made up for your absence,

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: for they have refreshed my spirit and yours. So give recognition to people like these.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: The assemblies of Asia greet you. Aquila and Prisca greet you warmly in the Lord, together with the assembly that meets in their house.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: All the brothers and sisters greet you. Greet one another with a holy kiss.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: The greeting is in my own hand—Paul’s.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: If anyone does not love the Lord, let that person be accursed. Our Lord, come!

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: The grace of the Lord Jesus be with you.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: My love be with all of you in Christ Jesus.

notes.note: The word is used of all believers as people set apart for God, echoing the Septuagint's language for Israel. 'Saints' now suggests canonised individuals or people of exceptional virtue, which is not the sense here. Many translations keep 'saints'; others use 'God's people'. Here it refers specifically to the believers in Jerusalem, for whom the collection was being gathered.

A first-century hearer knew this word as the term for a civic gathering and as the Septuagint's word for Israel assembled. 'Church' is the near-universal rendering and is clear in reference, but it now suggests a building or an institution. 'Assembly' is used throughout this translation so that the reader can see it is one Greek word.

notes.phrase: On the first day of every week
notes.note: The Greek follows the Jewish way of counting days from the Sabbath, literally 'on day one of the sabbath-week', which is Sunday. The instruction is for each person to set money aside privately ('at home' is literally 'with himself'). Whether the choice of day reflects a weekly gathering of the community on Sunday is plausible but not stated.

The Greek phrase 'by means of letters' can attach to either verb. Most modern translations take it as here: Paul will send the approved delegates with letters of introduction. The alternative, found in some older versions, is that the Corinthians approve their delegates by letter ('whomever you approve by your letters').

This is the same Greek word translated 'grace' in verse 23. It covers favor, generosity and the concrete gift that expresses them. Paul uses it repeatedly for the Jerusalem collection, especially in 2 Corinthians 8–9.

notes.phrase: he was not at all willing
notes.note: The Greek says literally 'it was not at all will that he come now', without saying whose will. Most translations take it as Apollos's own unwillingness, as here. Some interpreters understand it as God's will, since the word used absolutely can carry that sense. The following clause, 'he will come when he has the opportunity', slightly favors the first reading.

The verb is formed from the word for 'man', and older versions render it 'quit you like men' or 'act like men'. In the Septuagint it is the standard exhortation to courage, usually paired with 'be strong' as it is here (for example, in the charge to Joshua). It is addressed to the whole community, and the point is bravery and not maleness. Several modern translations render it this way.

The Greek masculine plural was the normal way to address a mixed group of siblings or fellow members, and the Corinthian community plainly included women. Where the whole community is meant, this translation uses 'brothers and sisters', as several modern versions do. In verses 11 and 12, where specific travelling companions are meant, 'the brothers' is kept.

Paul plays on two related verbs: Stephanas's household have 'placed themselves' at the service of others (verse 15), and the Corinthians are to 'place themselves under' such people. The traditional 'submit' or 'be subject' is accurate in sense but loses the echo. The call is to voluntary deference toward those who do the work, not to a formal chain of command.
This is the Roman province of Asia, the western part of what is now Turkey, with Ephesus as its chief city. It is not the continent. Paul is writing from Ephesus (verse 8).

Letters were normally dictated to a scribe. At this point Paul takes the pen and writes the closing lines himself, which served as a personal touch and as a mark of authenticity. He does the same at the end of several other letters.

Paul writes an Aramaic phrase in Greek letters without translating it, which suggests it was a fixed prayer inherited from the earliest Aramaic-speaking believers. Divided as marana tha, as in the Greek text followed here, it is a prayer: 'Our Lord, come!' Divided as maran atha it would be a statement: 'Our Lord has come' or 'is coming'. Most scholars prefer the prayer, in part because Revelation 22:20 has a similar prayer in Greek. Older versions leave the Aramaic untranslated.

candidates.rendering: brothers and sisters (mixed community) / brothers (specific men)
candidates.reason: The plural occurs hundreds of times across the letters and Acts, and whether to render it inclusively needs one policy so readers do not see it vary by chapter.
The word ranges over grace, favor, gift and thanks throughout the New Testament, and the boundaries between these renderings should be fixed once.
It recurs in household codes and in passages on civil authority, where 'submit', 'be subject' and 'defer' carry noticeably different tones.
It is very frequent, and translators vary among urge, appeal, exhort, encourage and comfort, so the sense boundaries need a single decision.
It recurs in Romans 9:3, 1 Corinthians 12:3 and Galatians 1:8-9, where translations vary among 'accursed', 'under a curse' and the loanword 'anathema'.
